input.question: Who takes over essential jobs during a strike?
input.ground_truth: If you are referring to essential services such as police, firemen, emergency rescue etc, in many jurisdictions it is actually illegal for them to strike. For example in New York State the Public Employees Fair Employment Act has banned all public employees from striking since 1967, and in the UK the 1919 Police Act bans all police from going on strike. In exchange, many of these laws have a binding arbitration clause in case of an impasse in labor negotiations.

Okay! Imagine you and your friends are playing a game at school, but you all decide to take a break and not play for a while to ask for better toys. Who will take care of the game while you are on your break? Maybe the teachers or other kids who weren’t playing before will help out until you come back.

In a strike, workers stop working together to ask for better things, like more playtime or better snacks. While they are not working, someone else—maybe other workers, machines, or sometimes even volunteers—steps in to do the important jobs so everything doesn’t stop completely. These people are called “scabs” or “replacement workers,” but sometimes other people just help out to keep things running.
